#10073. Hospital gave very sick doctor a special PC for his personal, erm, pleasure

Support chap told to either allow blatant policy violations or find a new job

Welcome to Friday and therefore to a fresh edition of On Call, The Register's weekly tale of tech support trials and tribulations that readers kindly share.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Mason," who told us he once worked at a hospital doing tech support for its research labs.

"One of the labs was for a doctor who was one of the world's top organ transplant researchers" Mason told On Call.

The doctor was also a voracious consumer of – ahem – adult entertainment, a habit that saw his PC and other machines around the lab often come down with a nasty case of malware.

Mason got to clean that up, sometimes multiple times in a single week.

The doctor's foibles were widely known around the hospital, as was the fact that his activities violated several workplace policies.

Mason pointed this out to his boss every time he cleaned up a fresh malware outbreak but such was the doctor's status that management never intervened.

And then the hospital was hit by a nasty cyber-worm that did a lot of damage. During the cleanup, Mason's colleagues found logs that showed the doctor's PC was the source of the infection, and that he had been indulging in his online hobby at the time the worm arrived.

Mason assumed this would be the moment at which the doctor would finally be held accountable and face disciplinary action.

Instead the doctor made a bargain with the IT department to henceforth use only a designated PC when pursuing – ahem – personal and/or intimate matters. And he would only use office PCs for actual work.

The hospital's tech team rescued a PC from its e-waste pile for this job.

"Get this thing going and deliver it to Doctor Pervert," Mason's boss ordered.

By this stage, Mason had had enough. He escalated his protests, telling his boss that indulging this doctor was unprofessional, likely exposed the hospital to lawsuits, wasted IT department resources, and was just wrong.

"What do you want to hear?" his boss replied. "The CIO told me do this or get another job."

After Mason prepped that PC, he only needed to clean up malware about once a year – after the poor machine was so overrun with malware that it no longer served the doctor's purposes.

Mason left the hospital while this PC was still in place.

"You'll be shocked, no doubt, to learn that years later the doctor's graduate students filed a lawsuit," he told On Call. "And that the separate fun-time computer was one of the pieces of evidence that the hospital knew about his – ahem – proclivities and not just ignored them but facilitated them."

Have you been asked to cover up revolting behavior? Or ignore policy? Click here to share your story with On Call. It's our policy to tell a great tech support story week, so we appreciate every contribution. ®

#10071. Security incident disclosure — July 2026

Earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure. This one was different from anything we had handled before in one important way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system - and we detected and dissected it largely with AI of our own.

We identified unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and to several credentials used by our services. We are still completing our assessment of whether any partner or customer data was affected, and we will contact any affected parties directly as required. We have found no evidence of tampering with public, user-facing models, datasets, or Spaces, and our software supply chain (container images and published packages) was verified clean.

The intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline. A malicious dataset abused two code-execution paths in our dataset processing (a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection in a dataset configuration) to run code on a processing worker. From there, the actor escalated to node-level access, harvested cloud and cluster credentials, and moved laterally into several internal clusters over a weekend.

The campaign was run by an autonomous agent framework (appearing to be built on an agentic security-research harness - used LLM still not known) executing many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control staged on public services. This matches the "agentic attacker" scenario the industry has been forecasting.

We are working with outside cybersecurity forensic specialists to investigate the issue and review our security policies and procedures. Finally, we have also reported this incident to law enforcement agencies.

As a precaution, we recommend rotating any access tokens and reviewing recent activity on your account. If you believe you are affected, or want to report a security concern, contact us at security@huggingface.co.

We are grateful to the teams across Hugging Face who responded around the clock, and we are sorry for any disruption this caused. Security is never finished; we will keep raising the bar.

The attack was initially surfaced through AI-assisted detection. Our anomaly-detection pipeline uses LLM-based triage over security telemetry to separate real signals from the daily noise, and it was the correlation of those signals that flagged the compromise.

To understand what a swarm of tens of thousands of automated actions did, we ran LLM-driven analysis agents over the full attacker action log, comprised of more than 17,000 recorded events. This allowed us to reconstruct the timeline, extract indicators of compromise, map the credentials touched, and separate genuine impact from decoy activity. Thanks to this approach, we were able to do in hours what would usually take days, and match the adversary's speed.

The choice of models we could use for this analysis was constrained in a way we did not anticipate; we describe this below.

When we started the log analysis, we first used frontier models behind commercial APIs. This did not work: the analysis requires submitting large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and C2 artifacts, and these requests were blocked by the providers' safety guardrails, which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker. We ran the forensic analysis instead on zai-org/GLM-5.2, an open-weight model, on our own infrastructure. This had a second benefit: no attacker data, and none of the credentials it referenced, left our environment.

This experience points to a gap worth planning for. We do not know which model powered the attacker's agents, whether a jailbroken hosted model or an unrestricted open-weight one; either way, the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried. The practical lesson for defenders: have a capable model you can run on your own infrastructure vetted and ready before an incident, both to avoid guardrail lockout and to keep attacker data and credentials from leaving your environment. This is not an argument against safety measures on hosted models, and we are sharing this feedback with the providers concerned.

Autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical. It lowers the cost of running a broad, patient, multi-stage campaign, and it operates at machine speed. Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface, and using AI on defense to keep pace. We will keep investing there, and keep sharing what we learn.

#10070. Safari's Autofill feature may be distorting time

Repeated reports about inaccurate form filling have lingered for years

The autofill feature of Apple's Safari browser appears to be suffering from a date handling error that occasionally leads it to supply an incorrect credit card expiration date when filling out forms.

The supposed issue has been a sore spot for Apple customers dating back at least to 2017, when the author of an Apple Community forum post complained about changes to the month field in the Autofill credit card expiration date when moving between time zones.

"I've noticed for the last year or so, whenever I travel from Eastern time zone (my home) to Central time zone or even Pacific time zone that my credit card expiration date month changes in Safari Autofill," the Safari user wrote.

Another post in 2021 raised similar concerns.

"I don't know how to reproduce this," the author wrote. "Every few months Safari on any of my devices changes the expiration month of all of my stored credit cards by decreasing the month by 1, for example instead of 10/2029 it changes it to 09/2029."

Three years later, another person posting to Apple's Community forum reported the same issue.

"For a few years now every time I use Autofill on my computer my credit cards (ALL of them) always have their expiration dates change one month earlier," the 2024 post says. "I thought it was just a glitch on my computer but I bought a new computer and didn't transfer anything from my old one and it is still doing it."

An unrelated Autofill bug report from 2024 suggests that if there is an issue, it resides in Apple-owned Safari code rather than Safari's open source WebKit engine.

Wherever the bug may reside, Safari's unreliable handling of credit card dates has kept a complaint-filled Reddit thread going for four years. And the reported month-shifting has been noted in other threads, too.

The Register was unable to reproduce the described behavior, but a reader insists it's still a problem.

"The Safari AutoFill feature sometimes fills in the credit card expiration date wrong," the reader explained. "My credit card expires in December, but sometimes Apple helpfully enters November."

"To be clear, the card is stored correctly when inspected in Settings," our tipster added. "The off-by-one error only happens when filling out a form in Safari, and not consistently."

One possible way this might happen is if the Safari Autofill code implemented the expiration date using Swift's DateComponent type and stored it as a Calendar object with UTC as the TimeZone identifier. Doing so would anchor the date to a specific time. If the date components were extracted in Pacific Time, the value would be represented as eight hours ahead (PST). So 9/1/2027 at 00:00 would appear as 8/31/2027 at 16:00.

Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but we're told Apple's Help Desk – or "Helpless Desk" as our source put it – advised clearing the browser cache and re-entering details of the affected credit card.

If that works, it suggests Safari's handling of cached data in the context of Autofill dates may need to be revisited.

Apple does not maintain a public bug database and the community-maintained OpenRadar sheds no light on these reports. ®

#10069. Newer Models, Same Advantage

Three months ago, we published a paper on DharmaOCR and open-sourced one of the models. The objective was specific: optical character recognition engineered for Brazilian Portuguese.

The training pipeline was built in two stages. The first was a supervised fine-tuning step, drawing on a broad collection of Portuguese-language files from different sources, formats, and levels of complexity. This stage aligned the model's weights to the specific vocabulary, syntax, and document structures of Brazilian Portuguese — concentrating representational capacity on the target language rather than distributing it across a broader multilingual space. The second stage applied Direct Preference Optimization: rather than training only on correct transcriptions, the model learned from comparative preference data between competing outputs, teaching it to consistently select the better extraction at inference time. This stage addressed a different problem: not accuracy, but stability. By suppressing the failure modes that cause generative models to produce repetitive or incoherent output, DPO reduced inference time and cost, and materially improved the reliability of what the model delivered in production.

The combined result was a model that achieved the highest extraction quality score with the lowest degeneration rate on a Portuguese-focused benchmark. Both stages were necessary. The fine-tuning stage built domain competency; the DPO stage ensured that competency held under the conditions where models tend to fail.

OCR models have been moving quickly. But the gaps that originally motivated DharmaOCR's design (in extraction quality on complex documents and in model stability under production conditions) have not closed. They have, if anything, become more instructive as the field has changed.

The proliferation of multimodal generative models made language model-based OCR widely accessible, and the wave of fine-tuned OCR variants that followed reflects how fast that adoption has moved. That proliferation has not, however, changed the fundamental character of the technology. Every OCR system built on a generative model is probabilistic. Transcription errors are an inherent variable of this probabilistic technology. What differentiates models is how many errors they make and of what kind. That is determined by two things: the structure of the model (its architecture and parameter count) and how those parameters were trained for the task.

Architecture and parameter count establish the ceiling on what a model can learn. Training determines how that capacity is allocated.

This distinction is where specialization becomes a structural question rather than a design preference. When a model is trained on a restricted domain — a single language, a bounded document type, a specific task — All of its parameters are dedicated to that specific task. When a model is trained to cover a broader range of domains — a multilingual model handling N languages, for instance — those same parameters must be distributed across all of them. The distribution is not linear: the neuron superposition principle means individual parameters can encode multiple features simultaneously. But the division is real, and its consequences are real. A model covering more ground commits less to any given part of it.

DharmaOCR was trained to accept that constraint in reverse. The model is not designed to be the best option for other languages, and was never intended to be. In exchange, every parameter available to the network could be oriented toward the specific vocabulary, morphology, and orthographic patterns of Brazilian Portuguese — the most directed possible use of the model's resources for that domain.

That concentration is the structural basis of an inherent advantage over multilingual and broader-domain models. The advantage does not depend on having a larger architecture or a more sophisticated training procedure than competitors use — new architectures and new training techniques improve what any model can do. It depends on where those resources are directed: at one domain rather than spread across many.

Three months later, newer models have arrived. Whether the case for specialization holds when those models are newer and more capable is a different question.

Three months after the DharmaOCR paper appeared, two new OCR models attracted significant attention from the research community: Mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR. Both represent genuine technical advances — new training techniques, new datasets, and strong results across multiple languages on a range of benchmark evaluations. They are the kind of models that raise the competitive standard for what OCR systems are expected to deliver.

When we ran both against the DharmaOCR benchmark — an evaluation designed exclusively around Portuguese — the results were conclusive.

DharmaOCR scored 0.925. Mistral OCR4 scored 0.798. Unlimited-OCR scored 0.7587.

The difference is significant. Mistral OCR4 falls approximately 13 points below DharmaOCR; Unlimited-OCR falls more than 16 points below. Both were released after our model, both backed by substantial research resources. On a task where DharmaOCR's fundamental design decision was to concentrate entirely on Portuguese, the specialization advantage is measurable and significant.

The benchmark is the central finding. What follows illustrates why the gap takes the specific shape it does.

Processing non-trivial Portuguese documents reveals precisely where multilingual models tend to break. ENEM essays (Brazil's national high school examination) combine handwritten text with vocabulary, proper nouns, and cultural references that are specific to Brazilian Portuguese. They are exactly the kind of documents where language-specific training produces a return.

Figure 1: ENEM essay manuscript used in benchmark evaluation with outputs of the each model. Misreads marked in red.

Mistral OCR4, evaluated on documents of this kind, transcribed the name Chico Buarque (one of Brazil's most widely recognized musicians and poets) as "Chico Barque." Unlimited-OCR rendered the same name as "chico bique." Confronted with the phrase "O Brasil não exclui, assimila" ("Brazil does not exclude, it assimilates", a Chico Buarque quotation embedded in the same document) Unlimited-OCR returned: "a dose de chico bique, 'o Brasil no exclu, eliminila.'

These are not random errors. A model with insufficient exposure to Brazilian Portuguese does not fail arbitrarily — it fails at precisely the vocabulary and proper nouns that distinguish Brazilian Portuguese from the broader multilingual corpus. Chico Buarque is not an obscure reference; the name is nationally recognized. Its systematic corruption across outputs is not an edge case. It is a diagnostic: evidence of where the model's training did not go.

DharmaOCR, evaluated on the same documents, handles these cases correctly. The reason is direct: the model's training was concentrated on this linguistic space, orienting its resources toward the vocabulary and proper noun distributions that characterize Brazilian Portuguese rather than spreading them across many languages at once.

The examples illustrate the benchmark rather than replace it. The benchmark establishes the magnitude of the gap; the examples show why it is concentrated in language-specific recognition rather than in general capability.

Extraction accuracy, however, is only one dimension of production performance. Stability under visual difficulty is another — and operationally, it is the more consequential one to fail on.

When a generative model encounters a document it cannot clearly resolve — small fonts, degraded scan quality, dense handwriting — it faces uncertainty in its input signal. Models trained primarily on next-token prediction objectives face a specific vulnerability here: when the visual signal becomes ambiguous, the model can continue generating from prior learned patterns rather than from the source document. The result is text degeneration — output that is repetitive, incoherent, and semantically disconnected from the page.

Presented with a document with small fonts, Mistral OCR4 produces output with no connection to what is written.

Figure 3: DharmaOCR output and Mistral OCR4 degenerated output

This is not a low-quality transcription of the source. It is a failure of an entirely different category.

The operational consequence is distinct from that of a transcription error. An incorrect transcription is wrong in a recoverable way — it stands in a relationship to the source document, and the error can in principle be identified and corrected. Degenerated output has no such relationship. It cannot be corrected because there is nothing to correct toward. For downstream processes that depend on structured OCR output — document classification, information extraction, compliance workflows — degenerated output is not inaccurate data. It is structurally unusable data. The efficiency that automation was meant to deliver is negated at precisely the point where output stops being information.

Mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR are good models with significant technical advances behind them. The degeneration behavior described here does not define them; it identifies a specific failure condition that their current training has not addressed for this domain. The question is what a training pipeline designed to address it looks like.

In DharmaOCR, the answer is the DPO stage.

Supervised fine-tuning concentrates the model's resources on the target domain — the stage that builds the linguistic alignment described above. But SFT trains on individual token predictions: the model learns to produce the correct next token given the context preceding it. Under visual complexity, this creates the condition that produces degeneration. If an early token in the output diverges from the source document, each subsequent prediction is conditioned on that divergent state, and the output continues to drift. Repetition loops and incoherent sequences are an inherent characteristic in this context — they are the predictable result of an objective optimized step by step without accounting for the coherence of the full extraction.

DPO trains against a different signal. Where SFT trains token by token, DPO trains the model against the quality of complete outputs — teaching it to discriminate between competing responses based on the coherence of the full extraction rather than the accuracy of individual predictions. The effect is stabilizing: on documents where visual complexity would otherwise trigger drift, the model is less likely to commit to a divergent path, because its training penalized outputs that lost coherence at the extraction level.

The result is what the original benchmark demonstrated: lower degeneration rates alongside higher extraction accuracy, on the same documents where models without this training stage lose coherence.

The benchmark establishes what is true today. It is less precise about what will be true in two years.

It is possible — and likely — that newer models will eventually outperform the current DharmaOCR even in Brazilian Portuguese. Architectures will improve. Training techniques will advance. Datasets will expand. The field moves toward higher capability at every level, and there is no reason to expect that trajectory to stop. This is expected, and it is welcome.

What changes with each architectural generation is the ceiling on absolute performance. What does not change is the structural logic that determines which systems come closest to their ceiling in a given domain.

Available resources — compute, parameters, training data — are finite. They must be directed somewhere. A system that directs them at a single domain will extract more from them in that domain than a system distributing the same resources across many. This relationship holds regardless of how capable the generalist model has become. The gap between specialist and generalist may evolve as architectures improve. The structural dynamic does not reverse. We explored this principle in more depth in an earlier piece on why specialization continues to produce an advantage as AI systems advance (Why Specialization Is Inevitable).

This is what shapes how Dharma approaches what comes next. The objective is not to defend the current model's benchmark position. It is to remain at the frontier of emerging techniques — new architectures, new training methods, new approaches to alignment and evaluation — and adapt them toward the same end: a specialized system for Brazilian Portuguese OCR that makes the best possible use of available resources, at the lowest possible cost and the shortest possible inference time.

Better tools do not work against specialization. They expand what it can achieve.

Three months ago, we showed that concentrating a model's training on a specific domain produces a measurable advantage over generalist systems, including ones that are newer and better-resourced. That advantage held. The same principle will determine how DharmaOCR continues to evolve — not by staying fixed, but by applying whatever progress the field makes to a domain that remains fixed.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

#10068. How hard could implementing DTLS 1.3 possibly be?

In January 2026, I somehow ended up leading Pion's DTLS 1.3 implementation and building most of it. It was still mostly an idea at that point, and I didn't really know how DTLS 1.3 worked. Most of the people who ended up building it with me didn't either :)

Ten months and ~400 commits later, DTLS 1.3 is the default in pion/dtls:

I wanted to write down the lore of how this happened, and also explain DTLS the way I wish someone had explained it to me. So this is both, with interactive demos you can poke and break along the way.

If you don't want to read the backstory, skip to the implementation.

Pion's Plans for DTLS 1.3 issue had been open since February 2020, when the spec was still a draft. It became RFC 9147 in 2022, but nobody had the time it takes to actually commit to it, and every so often someone asked for updates...

Meanwhile, in January 2025, Sean DuBois, who created Pion and its libraries, told me (a nobody) I could co-maintain it with him and handed me owner access to the whole thing. Sean trusted me more than I trusted me :)

I created Pion's Discord server, reviewed PRs every day, contributed new features across the stack, and talked my friends into contributing. But I kept opening that DTLS 1.3 issue, staring at it, and closing the tab. For DTLS fixes and reviews were fine, but anything bigger felt like I'd create an RCE!

Then, in May 2025, Theo (Theodor Signebøen Midtlien) said in the issue that he'd applied to NLnet. The same day, Sean offered to review and merge everything, and to go knock on companies' doors for money if NLnet said no. NLnet said yes, and Theo announced the grant on August 6.

At the time, R Chiu and I were spending a lot of time in Pion's SCTP stack, the thing WebRTC data channels run on. She implemented RACK loss recovery.

Adriano Sela Aviles had also joined while working with us on Pion's TURN implementation, and sent really important PRs, but he and R had their own lives and were not able to go all the way with the implementation.

I'd read the spec once and was comfortable with it from a high-level POV, so I was excited to help with reviews. R Chiu helped with the key schedule. But it was Theo's project, and while we wanted to help, we didn't want to get in the way.

People were waiting for it. In December, just as the project was starting, Justin Uberti from OpenAI, where Sean had worked, asked for updates. They wanted "reduced RTTs during connection setup, and also … post-quantum crypto support." Lower RTTs meant you didn't have to wait as long for voice AI to start.

Theo put together a high-level MVP plan and opened skeleton PRs, but then life got busy, including a new job at NetBird! By January 2026, I was starting a new WebRTC job at Upwork, but I don't have a family yet, so I have free time after work :) Theo was happy to hand me the project. I promised we'd do his plan right and extend it, including the parts outside the WebRTC subset. I wanted a real DTLS 1.3 library that Pion also happens to use, because users outside WebRTC need resumption, 0-RTT and Connection IDs too.

I don't want to get paid for my work on Pion, because I don't want to treat it as a job. I also wanted people to build it with me. So I asked my friends who had already contributed to Pion, Jade Kolos, Júlia Borges Paschoalinoto and Julia-Elena Roman, and later Jan Muška, to join the NLnet-funded effort, and recommended them to Theo. Then DTLS 1.3 was ours to finish :)

We had DTLS 1.2 extension parsers that didn't really understand DTLS 1.3, and an unmerged state machine skeleton. No record layer, no key schedule, no encryption, nothing that could finish a DTLS 1.3 handshake. And none of us had a real TLS background.

Roughly four months passed between the handoff and our first record-layer implementation. There were extension and helper commits, but the main implementation was stalled. We kept reading specs and other implementations: RFC 9147, RFC 8446, RFC 9146, IETF write-ups. I was still mostly anxious: I wanted to do this right and didn't want to break stuff people were already using.

Then Sean asked how it was going. That's when we got his backing to really go ahead. He helped with the code design (where DTLS 1.3 would fit with 1.2 in a clean way), the FSM, Go idioms, cleaning up some old code, and later most of the DTLS 1.3 ACK reliability.

But most importantly, other than the technical parts, he made me confident enough to build it and break stuff along the way. He told me I could merge stuff without review!

We didn't have to understand every last thing before starting. He reviewed, merged, unblocked and encouraged. Without him, I think this would've taken another year or more.

On May 13 we started the record layer. On June 19 we finally merged the state machine.

On July 7 I closed the six-year-old issue with this very reasonable estimate:

I think we'll have a working production ready MVP within two weeks.

The server's Finished verified on July 12, and on July 29 the client's Finished verified too. A Pion client and server finally completed a DTLS 1.3 handshake. On August 5 I got the first confirmation of DTLS 1.3 working in WebRTC against Chrome! I hadn't slept for two days, and couldn't believe it. I'd written most of it without testing against another implementation lol.

Our team's write-up has a line I really like: "Finished" is a different story. The handshake was just the beginning. August was more than a hundred commits: Connection IDs, KeyUpdate, HelloRetryRequest, SRTP negotiation, rewriting extension parsing, and a week deleting duplicated code that I badly underestimated.

We tagged the first v4 release candidate on September 26. Two days later I closed the tracking issue, and DTLS 1.3 went into Pion WebRTC's next major version. People outside WebRTC were already trying it on real IoT clusters. Seeing them pick up resumption and the other features motivated me to finish ECH and 0-RTT.

On October 14 I said support was complete. Before we released it, Anthropic rolled out their OSS scanner, and we sent pion/dtls through it. It found many old issues, but also new ones in the new implementation. Yey, we got to fix them before release!

On October 31, DTLS 1.3 became the default in pion/dtls. No more "not implemented" errors, examples using 1.3 by default, and 1.2 one option away. v4.0.0-rc.8 is tagged, final v4 is next, and Pion WebRTC's next major version will bring it to everyone who uses it.

So enough with the yapping! Let's dive in. But before we get into DTLS, what even is the D in DTLS? And how does it relate to TLS?

Everything on the internet travels in packets. What happens when one goes missing depends on how you're sending them.

TCP is a phone call. You get a connection, and everything you say arrives complete and in order, or not at all. If a packet gets lost on the way, TCP notices, sends it again, and makes everything after it wait until it arrives. You never see the gap, the conversation just pauses.

UDP is postcards. Each packet, a datagram, travels on its own with its own address, and it either arrives whole or not at all. Postcards get lost, arrive out of order, and sometimes the same one shows up twice. Nobody resends anything and nobody waits.

Here are both, carrying the same message, with the same bad luck:

Try it a few times and tap a packet or two in flight. TCP always delivers a perfect HELLO, PION!, but it can take longer to finish, because one lost letter holds up every letter behind it. This is called head-of-line blocking (and it's the boogeyman of the real-time world). UDP finishes sooner, but what arrives is a mess. The app can sort it if it numbered its postcards, but the lost ones are just gone.

The mess is fine for a lot of things, because for real-time media late is the same as lost. One can argue that an audio packet that arrives 300ms late is useless: the moment it was meant for has already passed. Video is even worse: a frame is usually split into many packets, and later frames depend on earlier ones, so waiting for one lost packet holds up everything behind it, the same head-of-line blocking as TCP. It's better to keep going and decide what's actually worth recovering.

WebRTC, for example, has a few ways to do that on top of UDP. RTP numbers every packet, like the postcards above, so the receiver knows exactly what's missing. With NACK, it tells the sender which sequence numbers it lost and the sender resends just those. That costs at least one extra round trip, so when there's no time to wait there's FEC (forward error correction): the sender adds a few extra parity packets, and the receiver rebuilds a lost packet from them without asking for anything. There's a whole post about FEC in Pion if you want the details.

That's why WebRTC tries(*) to send its media and data over UDP: it gets to decide what's worth waiting for.

(*) WebRTC can also use TCP transports, either directly with ICE-TCP or through a relay with TURN over TCP or TLS. DTLS is still used in both: with ICE-TCP the DTLS records are carried inside the TCP stream, and with TURN only the hop to the relay is TCP, and the relay usually forwards the same DTLS packets to the other side over UDP.

Anyway, the problem is that the protocol that keeps the internet private, TLS, was designed for phone calls. It assumes nothing gets lost, reordered or duplicated. Put it on postcards and it falls apart.

DTLS (Datagram TLS) is TLS rebuilt for postcards. To see what had to change, we first need to know what TLS actually promises.

TLS makes three promises about the conversation between Client and Server:

Mallory is the reason all three exist. She sits on the wire, which in real life is your coffee shop's Wi-Fi, a compromised router, a shady ISP, or anyone else between you and the server. Every packet goes through her.

You might think encryption takes care of the second one too. If Mallory can't read the message, how is she going to change it into anything useful? Try it:

Encryption alone hides what you said, but a stream cipher like AES-CTR just XORs your message with a keystream, so flipping a bit in the ciphertext flips the same bit in the plaintext. Mallory doesn't need the key, she only needs to know where 10 is in the message.

That's why every cipher in TLS 1.3 and DTLS 1.3 is an AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data). AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypt the record and compute a tag over it. Change one bit anywhere and the tag doesn't match, so the record gets dropped. Older TLS versions did encryption and authentication separately and got burned by the gaps between them more than once, so TLS 1.3 removed every cipher that isn't an AEAD.

AEADs need a key that only Client and Server know. But they've never met before, and every message between them goes through Mallory, so they have to agree on a secret while she listens to every word. We can explain it with paint:

✓ Client and Server match: yellow + red + blue, one part each.✗ Mallory is off: her mix has two parts yellow, and paint doesn’t un-mix.

Each side keeps a secret and only sends a mix. Mallory sees both mixes but can't un-mix them, so both sides end up with the same final color and she can't make it herself. In real crypto the "paint" is elliptic-curve math (X25519 is the common one), and "un-mixing" means solving a problem no current computer can solve in any reasonable time.

In TLS 1.3 the client doesn't wait to be asked. It guesses which key exchange the server will accept and puts its half, the key_share, in the very first message, the ClientHello. If the guess is right, the server answers with its own half and can start encrypting right away. That's why TLS 1.3 needs one round trip where TLS 1.2 needed two.

Key exchange alone doesn't stop Mallory from sitting in the middle and doing a separate key exchange with each side. That's what promise three is for. The server proves who it is by signing the handshake with its certificate's private key (the CertificateVerify message). Then both sides send a Finished message, a MAC over every handshake message so far (the transcript). If Mallory changed even one byte anywhere in the handshake, the transcripts won't match and the checks fail. Be Mallory and try:

Watch what catches her each time. If she touches the hellos, the transcripts stop matching, so the server's signature and the Finished MACs fail. If she swaps the key shares, she gets surprisingly far, until the server has to prove who it is. She can fake a key exchange, but she can't sign as server.example without its private key, and no CA will vouch for her own certificate. Well, unless she finds a CA whose private key is literally 4, which actually happened this October :)

That's how it works on the web, for example, where a CA says which certificate belongs to server.example. Standard WebRTC peers don't use CAs for authentication. Instead, each peer has its own certificate (which can be generated on the spot and self-signed) and puts its fingerprint, a SHA-256 hash of that certificate, in the SDP (Session Description Protocol) it sends through your signaling server:

After the DTLS handshake, each side hashes the certificate the other side actually used and compares it with the fingerprint from the SDP, which is usually sent over HTTPS or a WebSocket over TLS. If Mallory swaps in her own certificate, the hash won't match and the connection fails. In WebRTC both sides send a certificate, so both sides get checked. The catch is that DTLS is only as trustworthy as your signaling: if Mallory can edit the SDP, she can put her own fingerprint in it.

Some connections don't use certificates at all. With a pre-shared key (PSK), both sides already share a secret, for example a key that was put on an IoT device at the factory, and knowing the key is the proof of identity. The handshake keys come from the PSK, so without it Mallory can't finish the handshake as either side. It's a lot cheaper than certificates, which is why it's popular on small devices. More on PSKs later.

TLS assumes it's on a phone call, so it takes some shortcuts, and every one of them breaks on UDP.

It counts silently. Every TLS record is encrypted with a nonce derived from a sequence number, but the number is never sent, both sides just count 0, 1, 2... On a phone call that's safe. With postcards, one lost record means the receiver thinks record 5 is record 4, uses the wrong nonce, and every record after that fails to decrypt. Drop one record and watch:

nonce = IV ⊕ record number. The number itself is never sent.

Same nonce, but the record number rides in the header, in the clear.

One lost postcard and the TLS receiver is off by one forever. So DTLS puts the epoch and sequence number in every record header, in the clear. (DTLS 1.3 encrypts them again, more on that later.)

It assumes the handshake arrives. In TLS a lost handshake message is TCP's problem, in DTLS it's yours. Each side groups its handshake messages into flights and starts a retransmission timer. If the next flight from the other side doesn't show up in time, it sends its own flight again.

It assumes any message fits. A TLS handshake message can be up to 16 MB and TCP will happily stream it. A UDP datagram that's too big for the path gets dropped, or chopped into IP fragments that plenty of firewalls and NATs drop anyway, and the safe size on the internet is about 1200 bytes give or take, while a certificate chain is often several kilobytes. So DTLS adds a 12-byte header to every handshake message that says which message it is, how long the whole thing is, and which bytes this fragment carries:

ClientHello · 1,538 B · 2 fragments of up to 1,175 B

headers: 2 × (12 B handshake + 13 B record) = 50 B extra. TLS sends it in one piece with a 4 B header.

This one actually bit us. A retransmitted message is allowed to be fragmented differently from the original. OvenMediaEngine, an OpenSSL-based media server, splits its handshakes into tiny 256-byte fragments, and Pion's DTLS 1.2 reassembly assumed fragment boundaries would line up, so after a single lost datagram the handshake could never finish. Tristan Matthews fixed it by making reassembly track which bytes it has instead of which fragments.

Post-quantum crypto makes it worse. The post-quantum key share Pion sends by default is 1216 bytes on its own, so now even the first message of the handshake doesn't fit in one datagram.

And of course that broke something. wolfSSL, which a lot of embedded devices run, wants the first ClientHello in a single datagram so it can answer without keeping any state, and by default it just won't take a fragmented one. Most people using pion/dtls directly are doing IoT, so that's the worst place to break. Raising the MTU doesn't help either, the ClientHello needs 1415 bytes and plenty of networks can't do that. So now Pion sends an X25519 share next to the hybrid one like Go does, and clients put plain X25519 first so the first ClientHello fits again. If the server wants post-quantum, it asks for it with a HelloRetryRequest, so we still get ML-KEM everywhere it's supported. Clients with early data keep ML-KEM first, because a retry throws the early data away. I kinda get the X25519MLKEM768 hate now :(

It assumes nobody repeats things. Networks do occasionally duplicate packets, but TCP throws away bytes it already has, and if Mallory spliced an old record into the stream, TLS's silent counter would have moved on and it wouldn't decrypt. DTLS just put the sequence number in the header, so with UDP Mallory can record a perfectly valid encrypted packet and send it again as many times as she wants, and it decrypts fine because it is valid. So DTLS keeps a sliding replay window, a bitmap of recently seen sequence numbers, and drops anything it already saw or that's too old to tell:

Real DTLS keeps 64 slots. It only slides the window for records that pass authentication, so forged junk can't push it forward.

Now switch to "slide, then authenticate" and have Mallory send her garbage. One fake record with a huge sequence number pushes the window a million packets ahead, and every real packet after it looks ancient. That's why the window should only move after a record is authenticated.

DTLS 1.3 starts from TLS 1.3 and redesigns a lot of this. Let's go through the pieces.

My first big design decision was that a connection is always in exactly one of three modes. I wanted to make this super explicit because of a Firefox bug that broke calls to Pion: Firefox speaks both versions, and its fallback to 1.2 went wrong. We kept coming back to this for the rest of the year:

A lot of our hardest bugs were in that third one. Pick a client and a server and connect:

outcomes so far (click a cell to set both modes)

M: Mallory was stripping. B: the fallback bug was on.

Dual mode is tricky. The client sends one ClientHello that has to be a valid DTLS 1.2 hello and a valid DTLS 1.3 hello at the same time, and it only finds out which one it was when the server answers. If the answer is 1.2, everything from the 1.3 attempt has to disappear without a trace. Our first fallback didn't clean everything up. You can switch that bug on in the demo above. And Mallory can't force a downgrade either: a 1.3 server that gets pushed down to 1.2 writes DOWNGRD at the end of its random value, and the client notices.

A DTLS 1.2 record header is 13 bytes, on every single packet. For a video call that's a lot of bytes spent on bookkeeping. DTLS 1.3 replaced it with a unified header, where the first byte is a set of flags that say what comes after it. Poke the bits:

inside the lock: "hello"17 ← the real content type (application_data) now hides here, not in the header

It's smaller. The smallest DTLS 1.3 header is 2 bytes. The content type (handshake, alert, application data) isn't in the header anymore, it moved inside the encryption, so Mallory can't even tell what kind of record she's looking at.

The sequence number is encrypted. DTLS had to put the sequence number on every postcard, but that's also a tracking number for Mallory: she can count packets, follow a connection across networks, and measure exactly how much was sent. DTLS 1.3 encrypts those bits with a mask derived from the record's own ciphertext. Toggle "what Mallory sees" and click next a few times: the real numbers go 42, 43, 44, and she just sees noise.

It's mostly implicit. Only the low 8 or 16 bits of the sequence number and the low 2 bits of the epoch are sent, and the receiver reconstructs the rest from what it expects next. That only works because the receiver keeps careful state about every epoch, which brings us to keys.

As I wrote in the team's write-up: the names are scarier than the concepts. HKDF, AEAD, transcript hash, epoch, each is a small idea with a scary name.

TLS 1.3 doesn't use a key, it uses a whole family of keys, each derived from the one before it and each protecting a different part of the conversation. Encrypted handshake messages get one key, application data gets another, and after a KeyUpdate you get a fresh one and the old one can be forgotten. In DTLS each of these keys lives in its own epoch, and the epoch number in the header tells the receiver which key to use.

The thing that produces them is the key schedule, and it's built from one tool: HKDF, which takes some secret material and stretches it into as many independent keys as you need. You can try the actual key schedule here. It's computed in your browser:

server_​handshake_​traffic_​secretprotects epoch 2

Derive-Secret(Handshake Secret, "s hs traffic", ClientHello..ServerHello)

Encrypts the server’s EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished.

Click "new handshake" and watch every value below it change. One fresh key exchange at the top, and every key below it is new and unrelated to any previous connection. This is called forward secrecy: if someone steals the server's certificate key next year, they still can't decrypt today's call, because the keys never depended on it.

The other input is the transcript hash, a running hash of every handshake message so far. Mixing it into the keys means that if Mallory changed anything, the two sides derive different keys and just can't talk. I spent a good part of June getting that transcript exactly right. Miss one byte, hash a message twice, or accidentally include a retransmission, and nothing works. And nothing tells you why it didn't :)

In July we implemented the ciphers (AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305), record number masks, seal and open. On July 1 Pion also got X25519MLKEM768, the hybrid post-quantum key exchange. It does an X25519 exchange and an ML-KEM exchange together, so the result is safe as long as either one holds up. This matters because of harvest now, decrypt later: someone recording your encrypted call today could decrypt it in fifteen years with a big enough quantum computer, unless the key exchange already resists one. By August it was on by default.

Not everyone is a fan of ML-KEM, though. Daniel J. Bernstein, the person behind X25519 and ChaCha20, campaigned against an IETF draft that uses ML-KEM on its own in TLS, and says the NSA is paying to get it standardized. He calls the hybrid, the one Pion uses, "much more sensible". If ML-KEM ever falls, X25519 is still there :)

Reliability in DTLS 1.2 is pretty basic. Nobody acknowledges anything: if I don't hear back in time, I resend my entire flight, even if only one packet out of six was lost. And if the reply was lost instead, the other side resends its entire flight too.

DTLS 1.3 added an ACK message: "here are exactly the records I got." The sender resends only the gaps, and the receiver can send an ACK as soon as it notices a hole, without waiting for a timer. Same bad luck on both sides:

flight in 0.00 s0 records0 ACKs0.0 kB sent

Same flight in both lanes, so only the repair differs. 50 ms each way, first timer 1 s. Records ~250 B, certificate fragments 1,200 B, ACKs ~25 B + 16 B per record number.

After "Finished", it really was a different story: there's a whole second state machine for session tickets and KeyUpdate, with its own ACKs and retransmissions. So getting Finished to work still leaves you with basically another protocol to implement :(

In WebRTC, calls can use ICE to find a new path when the network changes (Pion has a post about that), so they don't need Connection IDs, but they matter for IoT users.

Without a Connection ID, a DTLS server finds the connection a packet belongs to by where it came from: the client's IP address and port. Now walk out of your house. Your phone drops Wi-Fi, switches to cellular and gets a new address, and the server has never heard of it.

With a Connection ID, every record carries a short ID that the server picked, and the server finds the connection by ID instead of by address, so your connection survives the walk to the car. Pion already had CIDs for DTLS 1.2. In 1.3 they're part of the core protocol and really different, so we had to rebuild them into the new record layer, while reworking the DTLS 1.2 implementation so we wouldn't have duplicated code.

Of course Mallory can make this a problem too. If the server just follows the newest address a valid record came from, she can record one real packet and resend it with the victim's address on it, and the server redirects the whole video stream at someone who never asked for it. The specs saw this coming: CIDs in both DTLS 1.2 and 1.3 already said you must check that a new address can receive before switching to it, but never said how, so many implementation didn't enforce this (including Pion's DTLS 1.2).

Return Routability Check (RFC 9853) is the standard way: before trusting a new address, send it a small challenge, and only switch once the answer comes back. Try the second half of the demo with RRC off, then on.

RRC has a fun backstory. While reading the IETF shepherd write-up for the RRC draft, I found this: "We have two different clients (Eclipse/Californium & Pion) that interoperate with a server." Someone had used a Pion fork for testing! I got so excited about that, I went and built a real production RRC for upstream Pion while we were still doing DTLS 1.3, instead of postponing it until after the release!

Pre-shared keys and resumption. If the client and server talked before, or share a key from somewhere else, they can skip the certificate work entirely. Smaller handshakes, less CPU, and still forward secret when combined with a fresh key exchange.

0-RTT. If you talked before, you don't have to wait at all. With a resumed session, the client can send application data in its very first flight, encrypted with keys from last time. Here's how the handshakes compare, and the catch:

Times are for the client's first application data to reach the server (handshake wait plus half a round trip). 1.3 adds a round trip if the server answers with HelloRetryRequest.

0-RTT data can be replayed. There's no fresh input from the server protecting it yet, so Mallory can capture it and send it again. That's fine for "show me the menu", not fine for "pay $10", so applications have to opt in and only send things that are safe to repeat. It also gives up some forward secrecy: go back to the key schedule, turn on "with PSK" and press "new handshake" a few times. The early secret never changes, because it only comes from the PSK, so anyone who steals that PSK later can decrypt the early data.

Encrypted Client Hello. TLS 1.3 already encrypts the certificate, so which site you visit is hidden, except for one field: the ClientHello carries the server's name (the SNI) in plain text, because the server needs it to pick the right certificate. ECH encrypts the real ClientHello inside an outer one that only names a generic front server:

secret-meeting.example, and it’s WebRTC. Noted.

While implementing ECH, I wanted our implementation to match crypto/tls, because I felt it was the right thing to do. But as soon as I started, I found two places where Go's own crypto/tls was too lenient with ECH configurations, and sent them patches (one, two). So we went back to doing it our own way, which turned out to be the stricter implementation.

I think setting up interop tests was the best decision we made all year. Testing Pion against itself only proves both sides share the same assumptions, so in April I created pion/dtls-interop and froze releases from main until interop was ready. It tests Pion against:

On September 28, when DTLS 1.3 went into Pion WebRTC's next major version, I added it to pion/browser-tests, which runs Pion WebRTC against Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Safari.

Anthropic's OSS scanner went through pion/dtls and sent us a report. On October 16 I opened #1228, "Fix all issues reported by anthropics/oss-scanner", and spent the busiest two weeks of the whole project working through it. Most of the real issues were in DTLS 1.2, session resumption and shared code that had been in production for years, not the new DTLS 1.3 code, and we fixed them on both main and the v3 branch so existing users can upgrade without changing anything. After spending so much time anxious about breaking stuff, that felt really good :)

sirzooro independently reported a few of the same issues (and others), found with Claude Opus 5.5.

There was one finding we couldn't fix in code.

Pion v3 lets you export a connection's state and resume it later, for example to hand a connection from one process to another. The scanner pointed out that nothing stops both the original and the restored connection from continuing to send. Both would keep encrypting with the same AES-GCM key and the same sequence numbers, and the nonce is built from the sequence number.

Reusing a nonce with AES-GCM is one of the worst things you can do in cryptography. Here's why:

same key, nonce A: same key, nonce B: (reused!)

✗ C1⊕C2 has nothing to do with P1⊕P2. It’s noise.

Slide the guess until the other line reads.

AES-GCM encrypts by XORing your message with a keystream generated from the key and the nonce. Same key and nonce means same keystream, so XORing the two ciphertexts cancels the keystream out and leaves the two plaintexts XORed together. Mallory doesn't need the key: she guesses a likely word in one message, and the other message shows up around it. The same reuse also leaks enough for her to forge tags.

Sadly we couldn't make the v3 API safe without breaking everyone who uses it, so v3 now documents loudly that a restored state must be used exactly once. In v4, Resume requires ExportState, which closes the original connection as part of the export, so there's no way to keep using both.

I'm really happy with what we built. I never thought I'd lead a project this big all the way to the end, and that still feels a bit weird. But the part I'm most proud of is the people. Whenever I got stuck, or talked about a problem for hours in our Discord server or group chats, someone was always there to listen and help.

None of this would exist without the people I built it with: Sean DuBois, Theodor Signebøen Midtlien, Adriano Sela Aviles, R Chiu, Jade Kolos, Júlia Borges Paschoalinoto, Julia-Elena Roman and Jan Muška. Thank you for all the reviews and testing, and sorry for how annoying I was about stuff I found cool :)

Huge thanks to Thomas Legris. He runs DTLS for a very large fleet of IoT devices with Pion on the server side, and at that scale every allocation per connection gets multiplied by hundreds of thousands. One of his PRs starts with "At scale (700k connections) - I detected some heavy allocations, especially at handshake." Over the year he sent a lot of optimizations:

Then he ran the release candidates in production, and they worked without a single problem.

Resumption got tested before it was even tagged, and I can't tell you how happy that made me :) ybaldus opened an issue about deadlines while building SWIM on pion/dtls, which "requires short lived connections and session resumption to be scalable." When I said resumption wasn't tagged yet: "Don't mind tagging it yet I can also use the current master commit." The report turned into a fix that applies read and write deadlines to the handshake.

Leonard (ltlobaro) did the same from the IoT side, where "DTLS 1.2 handshakes easily take up most of the device traffic". They played with the DTLS 1.3 resumption example, found that key logging didn't work with DTLS 1.3, and it was fixed in rc.5 the same day.

devArnoud ran DTLS 1.3 against a cellular modem whose TLS stack is wolfSSL baked into its firmware, and every handshake failed. When the server asked the modem to send its ClientHello again, wolfSSL sent the same extensions in a different order. The spec doesn't strictly allow that, but for compatibility Pion accepts it now.

enobufs tried DTLS 1.3 with WebRTC early and helped with the keying-material exporter.

Thanks to Philipp Hancke for testing DTLS 1.3 in his SPED implementation, which embeds the DTLS handshake in STUN, and for noticing that Pion sent a session ticket even to clients that never use resumption.

Thank you to everyone who reviewed, tested, reported and fixed things along the way. Thanks to NLnet and the NGI0 Commons Fund for funding work like this, and to the Anthropic OSS scanner team for the report that made v4 safer before anyone found out the hard way.

And thank you for reading this far :) Now go break something.

Come chat with us on the Pion Discord about anything.

P.S. Everything went perfectly except one silly mistake: I forgot to wire the message hooks into DTLS 1.3 after refactoring the handshake messages, and one hook was left taking a 1.2-only type, so we had to break the API in v4.0.1, our very first patch a few minutes later after we tagged v4 :(

#10067. Grabette: an open system to record robot-manipulation data

Record your own manipulation tasks in minutes with a handheld gripper, turn them into robot-ready datasets automatically, and help grow an open, collaborative dataset for robot learning.

Robot learning has a supply problem. We have capable policy architectures (transformer-based VLAs, diffusion and flow-matching policies, and even world models) and the GPUs to train them. What we lack is large, diverse, real-world manipulation data.

Teleoperating a robot to collect it can be expensive and demanding: first of all, it requires a robot. And depending on the teleoperation method, data collection can be tedious for the user if it takes hours and involve significant hardware and logistical challenges. That is difficult to scale with the wide variety of tasks and environnements required.

But you don't need a robot to collect robot data. Just a human hand, a gripper, a camera, and a way to recover the 6-DoF trajectory of what the hand did. Capture the demonstration and you have data a robot can learn from.

That's what we're releasing today: Grabette, an open, low-cost system for recording manipulation data. Pick it up, record a task with your own hand, and get back a clean, robot-ready dataset. No robot, no lab, no teleop rig.

And that's the bigger goal: if recording a demonstration is as easy as shooting a video, anyone can contribute. We want Grabette to seed a large, open, collaborative manipulation dataset. One no single lab could ever build alone.

Grabette is directly inspired by the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) from Stanford: a handheld gripper with a fisheye camera that records demonstrations "in the wild", recovers camera trajectories with SLAM, and trains visuomotor policies from them.

UMI proved the recipe works. Other (closed source) devices exists like Agibot's MEgo gripper, Genrobot's DAS gripper and Sunday Robotics skill capture glove. Our goal was to make it effortless to use, to get the barrier from "I have a task" to "I have a trained model" as low as possible.

Grabette is built into the modern open ecosystem: LeRobot for datasets, the Hugging Face Hub for sharing, and a processing pipeline you run from your browser with nothing to install. Grabette is something anyone can build on a workbench, use in the field, and contribute data from.

We have been developing Grabette for months, and we feel it has become usable enough to share. We are excited to share it now with you!

Grabette is a handheld gripper instrumented with everything needed to reconstruct a manipulation demonstration.

It carries two cameras, each with a distinct job. Splitting the two roles is deliberate: the cheap wide fisheye gives the policy the context-rich, wrist-camera-style view it needs, while the RGBD camera does the heavy lifting of robust 6-DoF tracking.

And while Grabette records data during tasks performed by a user, it relies on its robotic counterpart to execute the movements it has learned after training. So, meet Gripette, the robotic arm end-effector twin of Grabette.

Grabette hand held recording device (left) and Gripette robot gripper (right)

Components. Standard sensors you can buy, no closed pipeline, no fork lock-in. A Raspberry Pi, a standard Pi camera, an off-the-shelf OAK-D depth camera, magnetic encoders. The whole point is that anyone can build one from parts you can just order.

Robot-agnostic by design. Nothing in the capture or the data format assumes a particular arm. Demonstrations are stored as camera-local 6-DoF cartesian pose plus gripper state, the output is a standard LeRobot dataset on the Hugging Face Hub, so the same data can drive different robots and different learning methods. You will still need the matching Gripette gripper on your arm though.

This release enables anyone to go from "I want to demonstrate a task" to "I have a training-ready dataset" quickly and without prior expertise.

Press the button, and data from the observation camera, the tracking camera (color, depth, and IMU), and the gripper’s encoder joint values are recorded simultaneously, using a single shared clock to ensure proper synchronization. Press the button again to stop the episode, and the data is saved locally on the Raspberry Pi.

Open the Grabette dashboard in your browser. Select the episodes you want to add to the dataset, and with one click, post-processing begins.

Everything is now ready to start training!

A dataset is only interesting if it trains something. So, to show the loop end-to-end, we ship a complete example. But to be clear, this is an example of what is enables, not the product: the release is the recording system. Your Grabette data works with any method that consumes LeRobot datasets.

Our example takes 200 recorded demonstrations such as :

The data bottleneck doesn’t get solved by one lab, but by a community recording demonstrations everywhere. You can now help build the dataset: build a Grabette, record tasks you are interested in, and share them on the Hub. Every episode makes the open dataset bigger and more diverse, and every contributor makes robot learning a little less gated behind expensive hardware.

This release is only the start of the project! Grabette will keep evolving. We already have more coming, including Casquette, a head-mounted POV device to complement Grabette for egocentric capture (still a work in progress). But the most important next step isn’t only ours, it’s also yours: start recording, and let’s build the dataset together.

👉 Build a Grabette (GitHub) · Process your data (HF Space) · Contribute to the dataset

Convert Grabette recordings into LeRobot dataset

Hi Arita, good catch! It is now public : https://github.com/pollen-robotics/elec_grabette

#10066. Britain's tech ambitions depend on minerals made in China, MPs warn

Committee can't confidently tick off any of government's ten supply security tests, with alternatives a decade away

Britain's ambitions for AI, advanced chips, and clean energy rest on mineral supply chains dominated by China, and MPs say they cannot establish whether ministers have a credible plan to reduce that dependence.

The House of Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee has set ministers ten tests for securing critical minerals. Its verdict is hardly glowing – it cannot be confident the government passes any of them.

The tests cover whether ministers know which industries and technologies need protecting, what minerals they require, where supplies could be disrupted, and how domestic production, overseas partnerships, skills, and financing will close the gaps.

In a report published today, the committee warns that diversifying supplies will take ten to 15 years, and will require sustained investment and cooperation with allies. Completely cutting China out is neither realistic nor desirable, it says. Leaving Beijing with so much leverage is another matter.

Critical minerals underpin everything from batteries and semiconductors to datacenters and military equipment. The designation reflects their economic or security importance and vulnerability to supply disruption, rather than membership of an especially exclusive geological club.

The UK – like pretty much all major industrialized economies including the US, the EU, Japan, and India – is almost entirely dependent on imports of these materials and mineral products. But digging up more ore outside China would solve only part of the problem. The bigger bottleneck is processing.

Citing International Energy Agency figures, the committee says China is the leading refiner for 19 of 20 strategic minerals, with an average market share of 70 percent. A different flag over the mine does not necessarily mean a different route through the refinery.

The exposure extends beyond chips and batteries. As The Register reported in August, erbium is used to amplify signals in fiber-optic links, while yttrium goes into components including ceramic capacitors. IEEE Spectrum warned that China effectively monopolized the processing of both into the industrially usable materials manufacturers need.

That concentration has already caused disruption. China's rare earth export controls in April 2025, introduced following US tariffs, rippled through manufacturing supply chains and forced temporary automotive plant closures. British manufacturers can suffer even when Britain isn't the intended target.

The committee also highlights gallium and germanium, used in advanced semiconductors for radar, communications, and electronic warfare. China accounts for 95 percent and 93 percent of their global production respectively, according to the report [PDF].

Beijing flexing its leverage over chip materials is not new. China announced export licensing requirements for gallium and germanium in July 2023 amid tightening Western restrictions on semiconductor technology.

Yet MPs say the government has not clearly identified which domestic industrial and technological capabilities it wants to protect, making it difficult to determine which supply chains deserve priority.

Nor do import statistics reveal the whole exposure. Minerals can arrive inside batteries, magnets, and other manufactured components, disappearing from view as individual materials. Businesses themselves may not know precisely what lies several layers down their supply chains.

The committee wants confidential mapping and stress-testing with firms in critical sectors, followed by joint purchasing arrangements with allies to give new mining and refining projects dependable customers.

Committee chair Liam Byrne said: "Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy. We cannot re-arm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.

"Yet sixteen years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed. We don't know enough about what minerals we need or where to find them. Our energy costs make processing uneconomic, we're exporting valuable metal waste, and our public finance institutions are shackled by outdated rules."

The committee's five-part prescription is to identify the capabilities Britain must protect, map their mineral needs, expand domestic mining, processing, and recycling, pool purchasing power with allies, and establish a dedicated financing facility.

The proposed facility would bring together public funding bodies to back projects through grants, equity, loans, guarantees, and long-term purchase agreements.

"We're never going to eliminate Chinese minerals from our supply chains. But it's foolish to leave Britain exposed to economic coercion when we could be building alternative supplies," Byrne said.

"That's why we need a new Critical Minerals Finance Facility with the financial firepower to invest in new mines, processing plants and recycling, working with our allies to share the costs."

The report argues that existing institutions leave gaps, particularly for early-stage projects. It recommends expanding UK Export Finance's remit and allowing British International Investment to take equity stakes in overseas mineral projects.

Long-term purchasing commitments and price guarantees could help keep strategically important projects commercially viable despite volatile mineral prices.

There is also material closer to home. The report says 80 percent of UK metal products classified as waste are exported. MPs want better sorting and separation infrastructure, alongside more detailed trade data to establish exactly what valuable scrap is leaving the country.

For domestic projects, they recommend designated critical mineral clusters with permitting deadlines, help navigating approvals, energy support, and priority grid access.

Stockpiles could provide a short-term buffer too. The committee calls for an initial reserve covering approximately 60 days of minerals needed for defense capabilities, while stressing that warehouses are no substitute for diversified supply.

None of this offers a quick escape from dependence on China. The committee's argument is that Britain needs to decide what it must protect, work out what those industries actually consume, and help finance alternatives before the next disruption.

"De-risking even a prudent proportion of our supplies will take over a decade. Britain cannot afford to drift," Byrne said. "We must act now before dangerous dependencies become strategic liabilities." ®

InfoQ Homepage News Leapwork Play Reaches GA with Governance for Playwright Tests

Nov 05, 2026 1 min read

Leapwork made Play generally available on September 30, 2026 for teams managing Playwright test suites. The service adds requirement traceability and approval workflows around standard Playwright code, which teams can run in their existing continuous integration (CI) pipelines or through Leapwork's hosted execution service.

In its announcement, Leapwork says Play imports existing Playwright suites without changes. Engineers can connect Jira and Git repositories, along with product documentation, to build a knowledge base that supplies context for generated tests. They can also record a browser journey and turn the recording into a test.

Leapwork says Play monitors connected repositories for pushes that change application behaviour or the interface, then recommends corresponding test updates. Separately, its product page describes self-healing that fixes broken test steps instead of failing a run. The sources do not explain whether teams can require approval before a locator repair is accepted or how such repairs are recorded in the audit history.

For teams that need to review test changes, Play links each test to its originating requirement, ticket or document. Leapwork says the service retains authoring history and approvals alongside full execution logs, which teams can export as evidence. The service also reports flaky tests and coverage across applications or teams.

Role-based permissions and approval workflows control who can create and run tests. Leapwork includes the full governance, security and audit capabilities in enterprise packages, but the announcement does not specify which individual controls are available in the free tier.

Donovan Brady, vice-president of developer relations at Leapwork, described the management problem in the announcement: "What slows an enterprise team down now is proving where a test came from and managing thousands of them across dozens of teams once they exist."

Teams can also operate Play through an AI coding assistant using a server for the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Leapwork's product page names Claude Code, Codex and Cursor as clients and describes its hosted execution as Chromium-based. Leapwork says its hosted service runs suites in parallel, including environment and test data management.

Open-source Playwright already provides failure diagnostics through its Trace Viewer, including action details, network requests and screenshots. Those facilities help engineers investigate individual runs; Play's additional scope is central management of test provenance and approvals across teams.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness
